blocks.text: IN the hot Season of the Year, Madam, as you know the usual Time for taking a Walk is towards the Evening. Not long since, after a slight Supper, I directed my Steps to a small Grove; there, in the cool Shade, to enjoy the Sweets of the fresh Air and Solitude. I thought of nothing in the World less than of Sighing or Complaints; nay, I felt a certain pleasing Joy and Tranquillity of Spirit which I fancied nothing could have interrupted; when, behind me, I heard stifled Moans, Sighs and Sobs as of a Person in the last Extremity. I immediately turned my Head towards the Place from whence those plaintive Murmurs came; but I leave you to judge of the Surprize I was in, when I beheld that the Person who made those Complaints was my own Counter-part, my second self. In Effect, he was a middle-siz'd Man, plump enough, his Eyes tender and languishing, an innocent Simplicity in his Countenance, and to cut short, another my very individual self. You may well suppose my Astonishment was scarce expressible, to find my self become two; but it surpassed all Conception when this other my self, my Duplicate, accosted me in these Terms.

IN the hot Season of the Year, Madam, as you know the usual Time for taking a Walk is towards the Evening. Not long since, after a slight Supper, I directed my Steps to a small Grove; there, in the cool Shade, to enjoy the Sweets of the fresh Air and Solitude. I thought of nothing in the World less than of Sighing or Complaints; nay, I felt a certain pleasing Joy and Tranquillity of Spirit which I fancied nothing could have interrupted; when, behind me, I heard stifled Moans, Sighs and Sobs as of a Person in the last Extremity. I immediately turned my Head towards the Place from whence those plaintive Murmurs came; but I leave you to judge of the Surprize I was in, when I beheld that the Person who made those Complaints was my own Counter-part, my second self. In Effect, he was a middle-siz'd Man, plump enough, his Eyes tender and languishing, an innocent Simplicity in his Countenance, and to cut short, another my very individual self. You may well suppose my Astonishment was scarce expressible, to find my self become two; but it surpassed all Conception when this other my self, my Duplicate, accosted me in these Terms.

Look ye, Madam; I am not very much out in my Conjecure; nor amI, Heaven be praised, a Novice in the Art of Love. The Concern, the dear Embarrassment you was in when I discovered my Passion; your pretty manner of turning into Raillery my serious and fervent Protestations, and in a Word, every Thing, your whole Method of Proceeding, assur'd me I was not indifferent to you. But, alas! what am I the better for all this now? I am more wretched than if I had remain'd ignorant of my Happiness! You forget me! Traytor-like, you dissipate all my Hopes, and overwhelm me with Anguish, Confusion, and Despair! Return to your former self, I beseech you,'—And consider, that a Heart which finds it self slighted and neglected may become inconsistent: You change; it is very probable I may do the ve-

A surprizing Harmony cause me to go out of the Temple, and drew me to the Place from whence it proceeded. Twelve Tritons were walking on a Sort of little Sea and from Time to Time one beheld Water Spouts which pierced the very Clouds. A most agreeable Murmur joined with the Musick of Flutes and Hautboys, on which the Triton played with admirable Judgment. At their Head I saw P——founding his Bassoon. wondered at the Rencounter, and asked him the Reason of that Metamorphosis, and how from a Demi-Man it came about that I found him converted into a Demi-God? His Answe was, That the Nymph Amarillis had wrought that Change, and that they were now celebrating her Nuptials with the God of the Marsh. I intreated him to inform me where and who that Nymph was. He told me, she was approaching with her whole Retinue These Words were scarce uttered, when beheld appear twelve most beautiful Nayades playing on Lutes, Citterns, and other Instruments. That Beauty was then so charitable as to release the little captive Cupids, and then, loading me with their Fetters, she committed me to the Custody of her Charms, those terrible, remorseless taylors, who would rather, a thousand Times, suffer a poor Prisoner to perish in Bondage, than permit him to make his Escape. I was somewhat astonished at the Reception I met with: But reflecting on the Glory of suffering for so noble a Cause, I made to her a Sacrifice of all my Resistance, and embraced with Pleasure the Tokens of my Captivity.

We were led into the Hall of the Cupids, where the Wedding-Dinner was prepared, the Cloth being ready laid. This Room was adorned with abundance of fine Statues, Cabinets, and other costly Furniture, and set out with prodigious Numbers of precious Vessels, to be used at the Festival. The Floor was Ebony, intermixed with Veins of Silver. During the Repast, which wanted nothing either of Neatness or Magnificence, nothing was to be seen but Dancing and Rejoicing, nothing heard but Concerts of Musick, Vocal and Instrumental, with Acclamations of Joy, which, together with the Echoes, resounded in the Air, the more remote Echos answering to those nearer, insomuch that these Rejoycings were heard far and near. In a Word, every Thing surprized, every Thing charmed.

We were led into the Hall of the Cupids, where the Wedding-Dinner was prepared, the Cloth being ready laid. This Room was adorned with abundance of fine Statues, Cabinets, and other costly Furniture, and set out with prodigious Numbers of precious Vessels, to be used at the Festival. The Floor was Ebony, intermixed with Veins of Silver. During the Repast, which wanted nothing either of Neatness or Magnificence, nothing was to be seen but Dancing and Rejoicing, nothing heard but Concerts of Musick, Vocal and Instrumental, with Acclamations of Joy, which, together with the Echoes, resounded in the Air, the more remote Echos answering to those nearer, insomuch that these Rejoycings were heard far and near. In a Word, every Thing surprized, every Thing charmed.
The Feast being ended, the Company accompanied the happy Pair to the Chamber of Hymen, which was destined for the Depository of those Pleasures which that Deity had prepared for you. The Ceiling of this Apartment was of Gold enamelled, on which was represented the Amours of the Gods and Goddesses. The Floor was Mother-of-Pearl; and the Bed appointed for you was all of Ivory. After some Moments of Conversation, Hymen and the Cupids put you to Bed, and making us all quit the Room, they fastened the Door on the Inside, and partor with you of the Delights they had been preparing. of his faithful Flame! His Heart is racked with unspeakable Torments. Absence, with all its Train of Horrors, incessantly martyrize him. Dreads and Apprehensions devour him; and his Suspicions hurry him into an Abyss of uninterrupted Woe and Misery. An absent Lover's Heart fears every Thing; nor will it admit of any Consolation: The most terrible Ideas perpetually prey upon his Vitals; and to compleat his Wretchedness, a direful Jealousy reigns in his Imagination; and, in spite of all the Opposition he can make, it seizes on his Faculties. In vain he calls in Reason to his Assistance, hoping that will afford him some Relief, or Mitigation; its Efforts are ineffectual; and he soon finds his Diffidence to be so predominant, that it baffles and puts to Flight even Reason it self.

Judge, Madam, after all this, of the Pleasure I enjoy while deprived of your Presence! Would to Heaven, though at the Expence of my Life, I might once more approach those dear dangerous Eyes of yours: I should then expire with Satisfaction. My raptur'd Soul would joyfully take its Flight; nor should I envy those who enjoyed the ultimate State of human Felicity, could I but on those beautiful Hands imprint my parting Kisses.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: But now, in downright Sincerity, do not you blush at your unaccountable Laziness? And, can you find in your Heart to be silent any longer? Ah! Madam, learn to know the Folks your deal with. I am not a Jot less worthy the receiving now and then a few Lines of yours than are some certain Persons to whom you are very liberal of them: My Discernment is full as found as theirs, and I lay, perhaps, a greater Value on your Favours than they do. It is near four Years that I carefully preserve the only one you ever obliged me with; and I give you my Oath, that were I Alexander, your Letter would have the same Fate as had the Illiad.—After all this, Madam, reflect whether you are not more in the wrong than any one Person in the whole World, to debar me from a Satisfaction so justly and legally due to the Zeal I bear towards you; for I assure you, that, next to De Bauge, there is none I honour and esteem more than I do you.

blocks.text: From all this, my Friend, you may readily gather, that there is no very great Necessity, in the Situation my Heart is in at present, for me to search out Means of reviving an extinct Passion. Fair —'s Disdain now makes little Impression on my Spirits: It now nothing terrifies me. Her Rigour will now be quite out of Season; nor has she any farther Right in the least to impose it on me. Go not about therefore, to persuade me to sound her how she stands affected towards me, since it is far from being my Design any more to expose to her Indifference a Passion which she has disdained: Nay, even if I could have the Weakness to attempt to prevail with my self so far as to recommence it, you are too much my Friend not to use all the Opposition you are able. I have already had too bitter Proofs of that lovely Creature's Inconstancy, ever again to run the Risque of undergoing the Violence of her Injustice, and of losing the Sweetness of that State of Tranquillity I now enjoy.

blocks.text: Having thus said, she again issues out, and shuddering every Limb of her, advances, with deliberate Steps, towards our motionless Ambuscader. The Drole lies stock still; nor does he even scarce breathe.—'Ha! Doubtless, says she, the Traytor has received his just Reward!—Let me vent a little of my Spleen upon his hated Carcass.' Upon this, she dances round and round him, leaping and frisking over him, till she was pretty well tired, and then returns home in Triumph, chanting out Victory, Victory. She calls together all the Neighbourhood, inviting them to participate with her of the Laurels she had been gathering; affirming, That, by her single Prowess, they were delivered from their inveterate Adversary, the Cat, who lay sprauling not far from thence, whither she offered to conduct them.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: It was not long before Chardonetta grew pregnant, and soon made her fond Consort the joyful Papa of a little Chardonet, the prettiest Bird that was ever seen in the World, and the sole Delight of his doating Parents. As he was their only Son, extraordinary was the Care they took in the Education of this their Darling. With the greatest Pleasure and Satisfaction imaginable would his Father fit the whole live-long Day instructing him in all the Niceties of Musick, and the Progress the little Student made in that agreeable Science was such as surpassed all Hope or Expectation. In vain did the other neighbouring Chanters, envious of our young Chardonet's growing Glory, rend their Throats to reach his inimitable Lays: He ever bore away the Garland from all Competitors. This increased their Envy: They all mortally hated him, though, out of Policy, they all visited, carrressed, flattered, and highly commended him.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Our poor, afflicted Orphan bitterly bemoans his deplorable State. To be left thus in his Non-age, scarce six Months old, alone, solitary, and comfortless! No Bed-fellow by Night! Sitting moaping all the Day long without Company!—But, as Use makes all Things become habitual, Time wore away these gloomy Reflections. He finds himself Possessor of a large Fortune, and without Debts, Law-Suits, or Incumbrances: And as his Heart was wholly disengaged from either Love or Envy, his Hours glided on merrily and contentedly.—Happy might he have continued, could he but have kept himself and his Affairs in that desirable Situation! But our unthinking Bird had not long so remained, before he found himself overran by a Multitude of those quick-scented, pretended Friends, who never fail swarming about the Avenues of a warm Kitchin. They precisely knew the Time of going to Dinner, and not one among them all wanted to be twice asked to sit down at Table.

blocks.label: text

Then it was that our poor, too-good-natured Bird began, in earnest, to open his Eyes, and wheresoever he looked, nothing presented itself all around to his View, but the mean, grovling Baseness, the Malice, the Treachery of the vile Partisans of that Monster Envy, to whose venomous Malignity innocent Merit so often falls a Sacrifice.

54 To the lovely PALLAS.
Well.— We cut; he has the Hand; I deal; he takes five, and leaves me three.— I find in my Hand a Quint in Hearts, three Kings, three Knaves, the Queen of Diamonds, and three Spades which I discarded. A promising Game! Great Hopes! But, Morbleu! Not one Ace in the three Cards I took in!— Faith, Madam; I beg your Pardon for swearing; but it was so cursedly provoking, that I cannot keep my Temper when ever I think of it.
Sixty five? says he. Good. A Quint to a Knave? Equal. He then spreads out upon the Table seven Diamonds. Sixty five are seven, says my Antagonist, very gravelly; a Quatorze of Aces, fourteen more. blocks.text: These Words were no sooner uttered, but, with a decisive Determination, the vindictive Deity took Wing, without a Moments Delay, and with precipitate Speed urged his Flight toward the Abode of the friendly young Shepherd, and, armed at all Points, and well attended by all his most redoubtable Flames, his impetuous Ardours, and his keeneist Shafts, quartered himself in his, till then, pacifick Heart, nothing doubting of a glorious Progress in his Expedition. To make the surer of his Game, he assumed the Shape and Likeness of his Sister Friendship; and that good-natured, condescending Goddess, interesting herself in this Affair, which so nearly concerned her dear and only Brother, not only most readily equiped him with her Similitude, but a very considerable Part of his Success was intirely owing to her Zeal and Cordiality.

blocks.text: This new Votary of Cupid could, till this fatal Moment, approach the dangerous Object, his Eyes are now fixed on, without the least Palpitation, or Emotion of Heart. No Power had, ever before, those lucid Stars of hers, darting humid Fires, to disturb, or agitate the happy Tranquillity of his Breast. But now, the fatal now, alas! he finds himself absolutely incapable of withstanding their assassinating Glances. Fixed and motionless he stands gazing. Fain would he speak, but cannot: His Tongue is deprived of its Faculties; and in spite of the ardent Desire he has, and the Efforts he makes to communicate his insufferable Tortures to the insensible Object who created them, he wants the Power of Utterance, nor is he able to express his Sentiments otherwise than by heart-rending Sighs and Sobs, by which his Words are wholly smothered.

Rallying his dispersed Forces, he rowls on like an impetuous Torrent, routs all Opposers, and pulses to Conquest: Stupendous in his Progress, all things conspire to his Glory; Disdain is in Fetters, and Presumption, Mothered in the Throng, erects an illustrious Trophy to crown the tempestuous and invincible Conqueror, whose Laws and Ordinances are by none violated with Impunity.

She's robb'd of Peace, and defitute of Pity.

LETTER I.
Bemerton, April 25. 1699.
MADAM,
YOU have here my particular Thanks for your very extraordinary and obliging Present, which entertained me with great Pleasure and Wonder, and in which I can find nothing to censure but the Meanness of the Subject, though to confess the Truth that is my Fault more than yours *. You have, I perceive, a very pregnant Genius for Poetry, and, I doubt not, for greater Things, and if you will be advised by one, who has had some Conversation with the Muses, you should not employ very much of your Time in their Company, which in you would be better bestowed upon more serious and useful Studies.
God has given you a great Force and Strength of Spirit, and it is Pity, but that its Motion should be as well determined. I pray him to direct it upon the best Things, and in the best Way, remaining with the greatest Respect,
Your very humble and obliged Servant,
J. NORRIS.
* The Lady had sent him a Copy of Verses upon his Writings, which the Reader may see in her printed Poems. 8vo. Page 6.

GOOD MADAM,
LETTER II.
I pray, forgive my Rudeness in deferring so long my Answer to your obliging Letter, of which some accidental Interruptions, together with my late Indispositions of Health, have been the Occasion. I should very gladly comply with your Request, in giving you such poor Assistance as I am able, towards the Direction of your Studies, but cannot so well do it at this Distance, and upon that little Knowledge I have of you, unless you will be pleased to let me know what your Education has hitherto been in the Way of Learning, what Progress you have made in it, what Languages you understand besides your own, that so I may know what Books you are capable of reading, and withal what your Design is, and what Sort of Books they are that you would read, whether such as serve only to the Promotion of Christian Life and Practice, or such as tend more immediately to the Illumination of your Mind, and the Improvement of your Reason and Understanding in the Way of Science and Speculation. If you please, Madam, to give me some few necessary Hints concerning these Things, that I may not be altogether in the dark in what I have to do, you shall receive my Instruction and Advice. In the mean time, you have the Prayers and best Wishes of
Bemerton, June 12. 1699.
Your humble Servant,
J. NORRIS. N.B.

Corinna to Mr. Norris.
Reverend SIR;
I have perused your Book*, with great Admiration, and I hope not without some Advantage; but the Argument being too sublime for my weak Capacity, I dare not presume to give my Opinion of what so much transcends my Understanding. God being pure A&t, could not be Reasonably, and Philosophically said to Premeditate, or contrive before-hand; since every Thought of the Divine Nature was immediately Productive, and to Think with the Almighty was to A&t. It is also enquired by some, whether there may not be such a specific Difference in Thought, that a System of Matter fitly disposed, and organized, may be capable of what you call impure Thought, or Imagination; as being only the Operation of one Body on another, after a peculiar Manner. And as there are pure intellectual Minds without Body above us, so whether there may not be sensible Bodies without intelligent immaterial Souls below us. Since they say, it is not less difficult to conceive, how pure Spirits can apprehend sensible Objects without being united to Bodies, than how mere Matter duely formed, may perceive some Impression of Body, without the Intervention of an immaterial Soul. But granting a specific Identity of Thoughts, according to your Hypothesis, quite stops the Mouths of such Enquirers. I am sorry, I have not time to enlarge farther, as I could wish, who am,
SIR, Your most obliged Servant,
CORINNA.
LET

blocks.text: Need, and I beg your Pardon, for not answering your Letter (for which I thank you) so soon as I should, and indeed as I would, if I had not met with many Hindrances since I received it, which as I remember was no sooner than May Day, though it be dated the 30th of March. You cannot imagine what a Hurry my Life is, and what little Command I have of my Time, which instead of being free and intire for my own Use and the Service of my Friends, is lost and dispersed among a Company of Strangers, to whose importune Visits I am continually exposed, an Unhappiness, which I can more easily lament than remedy, but which my Friends I hope will forgive. As to the Objection, which the learned Person you speak of, is pleased to make against the Theory of the Ideal World, that it supposes Precogitancy in God; I grant it most readily, and 'tis what I contend for as a necessary Requisite to his Operations ad extra, or doing any thing without himself, which cannot be effected without some Preconception of it within, unless you will suppose God to act ignorantly, and without knowing what he does, or is about to do, which is impossible. But then I deny that all Precogitancy is an Imperfection. Indeed

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Precogitancy as it signifies a laborious and anxious Fore-thought or Contrivance, such as is accompanied with that intense Application of Mind, which we call Study or Premeditation, this indeed is an Imperfection, and such as results from the Limitedness of Understanding, and consequently cannot agree with the Perfection of an infinite Mind. But as for Precogitancy absolutely considered as it signifies only an Ideal View or Preconception of Things, this is so far from being an Imperfection, that without it, God could neither be what he is, nor do what he has done. Nor is it any Objection against Precogitancy in God in this Sense of the Word, to say, that every Thought of the Divine Nature, is immediately Productive, and that to Think with God is to Act. I grant that Thought in God is immediately Productive in Opposition to any manual Operation, or physical Motion, but not in Opposition to a Fore-thought, which must as Necessity intervene, or mediate. And so again, to Think with God, is the same as to Act. It is true, in this Sense, that God acts by Thought, and not by Motion. But it is not true, in this Sense, that all Thought in God is Action, and so (which I suppose, is what this Objection means) that there is no Thought in God antecedent to Action, or no Fore-thought. For that Thought whereby God acts, and which is indeed his Action, is Thought of Volition, and in this Sense to Think with God is to Act; but then there is another Thought in God which regulates and conducts, and in Order of Nature precedes this Action, and that is Thought of Perception or Idea, and in this Sense to Think with God, is Not the Same as to Act. And this I take

As to your second, I do not at present well understand it. It seems to me to be confused and wide. But I may consider farther of it, and perhaps may give you my Thoughts of it. I wish you well, and shall pray for your Health and Prosperity in the best Things, and remain with mine and my Wife's most affectionate Respects,
Your most humble.
and faithful Servant
JAN. 6. 1700.
J. NORRIS

THE continuance of your Kindness to a Stranger, to one who has nothing to recommend her to your Esteem, nothing that can satisfy entitle her to those Encomiums you are leased to give her, raises my Wonder, and I look on it as the Result of an uncommon Gerosity, of a more than ordinary Goodness of Temper: You take Delight in obliging, and estow your Favours with such an indearing sweetness, such an engaging Civility, that 'tis impossible to receive them without being sensibly touched by them; they make a deep Impression on the Mind, and with an agreeable Violence constrain the Persons on whom they are conferred, to become your Debtors, among which Number, I must own my self to be one: Yes, Madam, you have laid so many Obligations on me, that you have put it out of my Power to make you a Requital: I have nothing to offer you in Return but Thanks, and hearty and sincere Acknowledgment, which desire you to accept, as being the only Retribution I am yet capable of making you. The Correspondence you have so obligingly begun, shall (if you please to continue it) prove as lasting as our Lives, and I shall think my self very happy in the Conversation and Friendship of so ingenious a Person. I was troubled to hear of the melancholly Occasion of your Silence; the Kindness with which you treat me,

blocks.text: most agreeable Companions, and had I not be time accustomed my self to their Conversation, perhaps I should have been as unhappy as any of my Sex: But now, I thank God, I cannot only patiently, but chearfully, bear a great many Things which others would call Afflictions, Life and Death are Things very indifferent to me; I'm neither solicitous for the one, or afraid of the other; I know my self too well to be flattered into a Belief of my being any way useful to the World; my being out of it would prove no loss to any of my Acquaintance; they would find every where much more valuable Persons, such as would be more capable of serving them, and whose Conversation would be much more Entertaining and Instructive than mine. I cannot help pleasing my self sometimes with the Hopes of shortly leaving a World I've very little Reason to be fond of; the Thoughts of lying down in a silent Grave, of taking Sanctuary in a quiet undisturbed Recess, have something very delightful in them; but when I consider, that it becomes me to conform my Will to that of my Maker, and to think that to be best for me which he judges to be so; I blame my self for giving Way to such Thoughts, and resolve to be sedate and easy under every Circumstance of Life, and to employ my leisure Hours in improving my Mind, in enlarging my Understanding, and in making some Progress in the useful Parts of Learning: Morality has been my chief Study since I saw you; the Essays I've writ, are on Knowledge, Friendship, Life, Death, Humility, Grief, and on several other Subjects; you shall see them if I come to London this Winter, but that I believe I shall not, because

By HENRY SAINT JOHN, Esq; * (Now Lord Viscount Bolingbroke.)
I.
LONG have I wander'd from the Mufes Seat,
Where, ever present to the Poets Eyes, A thousand grateful Objects rise, Where all is gay, and all is sweet.
* An Incorrect Copy of this Poem was published in the Year 1701.
Where,

blocks.label: paragraph_title
blocks.text: ALMAHIDE. 117

paragraphs.text: ALMAHIDE. 117

blocks.label: text
blocks.text:
Where, when past Images we find,
By Memory with these combin'd,
She from her Store of fading Sense can move,
And frame no Fancy but of Joy and Love.
Where ev'ry Muse, and ev'ry Grace resides,
The sacred Temple where Apollo hides,
From the prophane, and vulgar Eyes,
His awful Mysteries.
This blooming Garden of the Delian God
Long since I left, new Paths to try;
On rough uneven Ground I trod,
And sought the gloomy dark Abode
Of Wisdom and Philosophy.

paragraphs.text: II.

blocks.label: text

From hence escap'd, with Joy to Thee I come,
Thee I re-visit now, my native Home.
That Magick Land no more I'll tread,
Nor drink of those Lethargick Streams,
That with their Poison taint the Blood,
And stop the sprightly Purple Flood;
That upward to the sickly Head
Send lazy Vapours, idle Dreams.
Again I'll taste of the Prophetick Rill,
Which rises fast by the Pierian Hill.
Phæbus all other Nymphs forsook,
To chace Caxtalia, young and fair.
To bathe in her delightful Waves,
All other Waters now he leaves.

blocks.label: text

Soar like the Theban Swan on high,
Nor be afraid to venture nigh
The flaming Region of the Sky.
IX.
Go on, my Muse, go on;
Boldly approach the Sun;
And from his Chariot-Wheel
Attempt to steal
The sacred Fire
That does the Gods inspire.
Then may't thou in immortal Lays
A more than mortal Beauty praise.
Or should thy melting Pinions fail,
And I precipitate descend;
Shou'd my unlucky Stars prevail,
And give my Days this fatal End;
Yet in the Monuments of Fame
I shall secure a lasting Name;
And to have dar'd a Thing so great,
Will place me far above the Pow'r of Fate.

XI.
In the World's early Days, When first Religion did appear; Religion, which has cost Mankind so dear; When Men began to raise
Gods to themselves, and then those Gods t fear,

Of ev'ry Virtue fram'd a Deity: Had Almabide been known, Had she been born to shine, They had ador'd no other Shrine, And she had rul'd the Globe alone.
All these Perfections are in her combin'd,
The Form of Venus and Diana's Mind.
Her Rays a Lustre like the Sun's dispence,
And shed on All a bounteous Influence
A cruel Glance from those fair Eyes,
A Word by her in Anger spoke,
Gives more Alarms,
Than Jove in Arms,
And swifter than his Light'ning flies, And surer than his Stroke.
Only below she cou'd not dwell, Or Hell wou'd be no longer Hell.
At her Approach the Realms of Woe Wou'd change their horrid Face;
The burning Flood forget to flow, And Furies fly the Place.

XII.
And fee ! the lovely Form appear:
Before my ravih'd Eyes!
Close to yon Chrystal Stream the Charmer lies.
Behold her, Swains, behold her there;
Impending Branches shield the Fair,
And Beds of Camomile the beauteous Burden bear.
See, how reclining on the Grafs.
In this clear Brook, her faithful Glafs,
First she collects her scatter'd Hair, .
Then in Treffes,
As the dreffes,
Places ev'ry. Flower that's gay,
Places all the Pride of May,
Not to adorn, but to compare.
In vain with her's their brightest Colours vie,
The blushing Rose
Its Weaknefs knows,
And vanquish'd Lillies own her Victory.
Nor raises she her Head, but downward bent,
Approves her Form, and smiling seems content.
Observe the Troops of Loves
That swarm about the Groves,
That I warm about the Groves, Lean on their Wings, and hanging in the Air, Mislake the Nymph, and think their Mother there.

XIII.
Gently, sweet Zephyr, gently blow, And make th' injurious Mantle rise, And wound our Hearts and please our Eyes. Unveil the Nymph, dear Wind, remove Those Clouds that hide this World of Love, And see the friendly Breeze obeys, Saluting he betrays.
Oh! give her Slave to know, That Sea of Milk, those Hills of Snow, And all the blissful Vales of Joy below. He wou'd, but can no more disclose, Resisting Robes oppose;
The thousand Folds of that invidious Vest, Inshrine their Treasure, and our Sight arrest Corporeal Eyes no farther reach; But Fancy is not thus confin'd;
Faucy can enter through the smallest Breach, And thro' the subtle Plaits a Passage find.
Thus having pierc'd the Screen, Fancy relates what she has seen, And tires the Soul while she instructs the Mind.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text:
In vain we hope to find a Cure,
No Remedy is nigh;
Without Relief we must endure,
And without Pity dye.
Fair Almabide Gives Love to All,
All that dare look her Victims fall;
But she herself Receives from None,
Or, what's the same to Me, from One;
One happy Man that dwells within those Arms,
Tastes all her Joys, and rifles all her Charms.
While dying Crowds of Lovers stand,
And look, and gaze, and wish to share;
But Virtue with her Magick Wand,
Encircles round the Happy Pair.
Thus when the Moon on Larian Latmas lay,
And rapt in Pleasure laugh'd her Hours away,
Her Beauty and her Light to all Mankind,
Without Distinction shin'd,
But to Endymion was her Love confin'd.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: The Shepherd Polemas, who, for the Strength of his Passion, as well as the Gracefulness of his Person, found no equal among the Swains, loved from his Infancy the charming Cyparissa: She might have passed for the most beautiful Nymph of the whole Forest, if young Lydippa had not shared with her in the Hearts and the Vows of all its Male Inhabitants. These two lovely Maids, by Force of their Charms, maintained against each other an undesigned War, of which the Shepherds felt the ill Effects. All the Graces seemed to have been divided between them: If Venus furnished Cyparissa with all her Charms, the Cupids fluttered incessantly about Lydippa; so that few Hearts could withstand those Eyes, in which the brightest Divinities had kindled up their own Lustre.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: But as these two Shepherdesses were the Delight of all the Villages adjacent, the most considerable of their Lovers deserve also a particular Regard. Polemas and Thamires were the only worthy of their lovely Mistresses; they both equally join'd to an Agreeableness of Person, a Delicacy of Passion, and a Livelyness of Wit. So that they inspired their Shepherdesses with a Tenderness equal to the Love they felt themselves. But as they dwelt not in the same Village, altho' not far distant from each other, they had not Opportunities frequent enough of cultivating between them that agreeable Friendship, which a Knowledge of their mutual Merit had given Birth to in both. blocks.label: text
blocks.text: How! Beautiful Nymph, said Tbamires faintly, dost thou shed Tears? And is it possible that the Condition from which your generous Cares have recovered me, should draw from your fair Eyes those precious Drops which ought only to fall for the Misfortunes of Polemas? One must be as barbarous as the cruel Animal from which your Valour saved me, answered she, not to feel Concern for the Condition I see you in; Love does not banish Gratitude from the Heart, and as upon this Occasion you have done for me all that you could have done for Lypidda, I confess I have done for you all that I believed I ought to have done for Polemas. 'Twas in this Manner that Love prepared these two Hearts to receive the new Impressions which he intended to fix on them.

Mean while Cyparissa's Lover returned with several Shepherds. They made a Kind of Litter, in which they carried Thamires to the Cabin of Polemas, where he was treated with extraordinary Care, and it was soon judged, that his Hurt, altho' dangerous, would be attended with no unhappy Consequences.
The News of this Adventure was soon spread all over the Country, but if every one else was amazed at it, Lypidda was almost struck dead with Sorrow; the Danger in which her dear Thamires lay, reduced her to a Condition which nothing but the tenderest Love could occasion. Sach was her Impatience, that she immediately traversed the Fields, in order to get at the Village which contained all that was most dear to her in the World; but her Strength

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Those who have loved very tenderly may imagine what was the Despair of this beautiful Shepherdess, never was any so afflicting: But Love, who without doubt directed all the Incidents of this Story, permitted this Misfortune to make Way for another, which proved to be the Henge upon which the whole Affair turned, for in the mean while a Lover of Lydippa, whose Name was Cafir, enraged to Madness at the tender Sentiments of the Nymph for his Rival, and the Scorn with which she treated himself, resolved by Force to make himself Master of her Charms, and carry her into some distant Country, where his Submission and his Love might at length make her forget the too happy Thamires.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Unjust Cafir, (cried he, advancing) treat with Respect the fair Lydippa, or I shall punish your rash Enterprize as it deserves. Is it by barbarous Violence a Man should seek to make himself beloved? In vain you attempt to restore my Soul to Reason, answered the impetuous Cafir, leave me to perpetrate a Fact which Love authorizes, or if your ill Stars compel you to oppose it, your Death shall soon insure the Success of it. I know no better Way of employing my Life, replied Polemas, than for the Defence of this beautiful Shepherdess, so that since you will listen to nothing but blind Rage, let us see if your Courage be equal to your Rashness.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: However that be, Polemas, having no more Enemies to combat, came up to the Shepherdess, and spoke thus, Charming Lydippa, what do I not owe to my happy Delliny? I have protected you from unjust Force, and the Defence of so good a Cause obliged the Gods to strengthen my Arm against this vile Ravisher. Generous Polemas, answered the lovely Lydippa, I owe my All to your Courage, you delivered me from a Misfortune more cruel than Death it self. But if any Thing could contribute to the Heightening of your natural Valour, 'twas no doubt the Desire of rendering Thamires the same Service which he had performed for you in the Person of Cyparissa.

The Resemblance of this Accident with that of Cyparissa, surprized every one; but nothing ever was so tender as the Thanks of Thamires; these two charming Shepherds who had reciprocally saved for each other all that they held precious in the World, carefled each other so tenderly, that this alone had been sufficient to express their Loves; while Cyparissa and Lydippa, embracing each other, swore an everlasting Friendship.

They left the Company unperceived, and changed Habits with each other. They were of the same Size, and appeared equally well shaped in their new Garments. Lydippa adorned her self with several Knots of Amaranth coloured Ribbons, which was Cyparissa's Colour; and this Shepherdess took in her Turn the Gridelin, which Lydippa was exceedingly fond of.
After this Precaution, which was necessary to prevent their being known, they put on their Masques, and returned to the Ball.

I have always loved you with the same Ardor; but I confess to you that I feel at this happy instant the most violent Pangs of Love. All my past Sentiments seem trivial to me, in Comparison of those which you have this Day inspired me with. Yes, fair Shepherdess, continued he, kissing her Hand, I adore you, and only Death shall raze from my Heart a Passion so tender, and Transports so moving. But to revenge this Piece of innocent Deceit, they resolved to pay them in their own Coin; and therefore withdrawing for a Moment, they changed Cloaths, and returned masquered to the Ball. blocks.text: But at length they began to fear left Polemas and Thamires might be offended with this light Raillery, and therefore resolved to appease them; in order to which, they sought them out in their Turn, and had not much Difficulty in finding them: The fair Lydippa advancing to Polemas, whom she mistook for Thamires, and placing her self before him, Oh! my Shepherd, said she, have you forgiven me a Frolick which occasioned the confounding Cyparissa and Lydippa? Ah! Thamires, pursued she, if you loved me now with so strong a Passion as you formerly did, could your Heart commit the Mistake? Would not yours by the Force of Sympathy have discovered which was the real Object of its Desire, in Spite of the Disguise which imposed upon your outward Senses?

blocks.text: My dear Polemas, ahswered Thamires, fighting, don't endeavour to look into my Soul, I am my self ignorant of what passes therein; but this transporting good Fortune as you esteem it, which unites me to Lydippa, is at the same Time ready to bind you to Cyparissa; how comes it then that your Heart still fights, and seems to wish for somewhat more? blocks.label: text
blocks.text: I see plainly, cried Polemas, that our Torments are of such a Nature, that we dare not communicate them, let us keep on both Sides our strange Secrets, and let us leave to Love and to Fortune the Care of concealing them, if we must remain unhappy; or of publishing them if these Divinities favour us. 'Twas in this Manner, these two Shepherds, without declaring any Thing, made each other sensible of their secret Passions, while the two Shepherdesses, laboured to conceal from each other the different Emotions which troubled their Minds. Mean while, Cupid, who intended perfectly to open their Eyes, revived the Country Pleasures, over which this God presided as Sovereign. If he armed the Looks of Lydippa, so as to give inevitable Wounds to Polemas; he placed himself in the Eyes of Cyparissa in order to triumph over Thamires: And by a just Equality he furnished these two Shepherds with Charms the most prevailing to inspire what he had inspired them with.

Polemas and Thamires, being informed of these Reports, took a Resolution to put an End to them, and without acquainting their Mistresses with any Thing of it, determined to go both to a small Temple dedicated to Apollo,, where his Answer might finally decide their Fates, and they mutually swore to each other, that whatever Sentence was pronounced they would submit to it without murmuring.

I believe it may be answered, that the Love which directed them gave them Assurance of an Answer propitious to their Inclinations. Be that as it will, they both went forth together one Morning, and having passed an intervening River in a Fisherman's Boar, they arrived at this little Country Temple, VOL. IV.

A Trunk of a Tree, which was hid under the Waves, so quickly overset the Boat, that there was all the Reason in the World to believe, that the unhappy Nymphs would be immediately drowned, if the Assistance of Polemas and Thamires had not prevented this disastrous Accident? These generous Shepherds threw themselves into the Water with undaunted Boldness, and swain with such Force, that each of them in a short Time got hold of one of the Shepherdesses, after which, making towards the Shore, they both got to the Bank Side, each laden with a Treasure of which as yet they did not know the Value. What then was their Transport, when Thamires knew that the Person whom he had guarded from almost inevitable Death was the lovely Cyparissa, and Polemas found in the charming Lydippa, her whom he had saved from the Fury of a treacherous Element. These Shepherds bestirred themselves so carefully about their Nymphs, that they soon recovered them from the fainting Fits into which the Fright had thrown them. Judge of their Surprize and their Joy when they found themselves again beholden for their Lives to those for whom they would willingly sacrifice them.

I say not this to put you in Mind of being kind to me; you have practised that so long, that I have a joyful Confidence you will never forget it; but to shew that I my self have a Sense, of what the Methods of my Life seem so utterly to contradict. blocks.label: text
blocks.text: Here and there one discovers the Plantations of a different Verdure from the Wilds upon the tops of Hills, sides of Mountains, or beneath in Valleys, many of them adjoining together, make a lovely Prospect. Over Head, a range of Clouds hanging very often not near the height of the Hills; the Sun exhaling so strongly here, and the Air so rarified, makes them side generally lower in the Atmosphere than. in the temperate Zone: And it is common to see them turn aside out of their Course, as if commanded by some magnetick Principle, to rest upon the Mountains, soon after breaking down into impetuous Showers; perhaps the natural Humidity of the Earth and verdant Woods, when approaching near by a simpathizing Principle attracts them; for it is observable, where the Woods are cleated, the Rains are less frequent.

I brought a piece of Oar over and had it smelted in London, which indeed produced only $ \frac{1}{27} $ Metal; but upon the Assay, proved very fine Copper. However, I believe there are very rich Mines in the Country, even of those that lie to the Day; nor can it well be doubted from those Indications that appear to the Eye, and the great Ponderosity; and it is highly probable there are many other Veins from the Steams that arise from some humid Places, the Taste of Waters, and their being strongly tinged, the Earth near them covered over with a heavy vitriolic Substance, &c.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: There is a fine fresh Water Lake at Mr. Abbourne's Estate, called the Farry; thro' it runs a large River, and full of Fish, Tortoises and Water Fowl, that affords very good Diversion for shooting from a Canoe softly paddled along by Slaves under a cloudy Sky, thus to pass from one little Island to another; in fine, Multitudes of Game are always in view, wheeling round over your Head, cowering low, swimming upon the Water, diving under, or rising from it with others, standing on the Banks, or wafted along upon little Heaps of Sedge: And thus the Tortoises are carried before you, or upon little pieces of floating Timber; the Expanse of still, clear Water discovering ten thousand Fishes, great and small, beneath you. The Noise of the Water Fowl, with the chattering of those upon the Trees and Hills around you, like harsh Notes to sweeten the Melody of the numerous Songkind warbling every where, made still more sweet by the cooing of the wild Pigeons and murmuring of the Turtles, among those thick shadowing Arches of the Forest that hang over your Head upon the Borders; the lovely Land-skip, all concur to make this Solitude of Pleasure extreamly charming.

There are others may be called Lakes or Ponds, very high up in the Mountains (like great Reservoirs) pent in by them, so have no discharge.
The Lagunes are all near the Shore, and have a Communication with the Sea, are sometimes salt, and sometimes brackish Water. In one of them, near Port-Royal, great Quantities of Salt is made. In those the Alligators and Guinas mostly frequent, which tho' Amphibious feldom venture out far for Prey, the Generation is oviparous, covering the Eggs with Sand, to be hatched by the heat of the Sun.
In the Woods and remote Savanaks are wild Horses, Cows, Hogs, &c. whose Flesh is very delicate eating, some wild Goats : These are all the Property of any that can take them; nor is any body denied hunting, fishing or fowling, where he pleases.

blocks.text: Jamaica may be valued at 15 or 18 per Cent. more than the Barbadoes, and perhaps 25 per Cent. or more, above that of the other Islands: Their Indigo better than any other made by the English; the Cotton very good; and the Cocoa-Nuts make such over rich and oily Chocolate, they are often forced to mix them with Caracca. Pimento is no where beside gathered in Quantities for Exportation that I know of; but here the Soil and Clime are so propitious, they might grow Trees to over-stock the World with this Spice, at little Labour and Expence.

text:
MISCELLANIES. 21
To Mr. CURLL.
SIR,
AFTER the most diligent Search I can make among my Papers, I have not yet been able to find the Alt of the Duke of Wharton's Tragedy of Mary Queen of Scots. I am pretty much engaged in the Country at present, but hope I shall have an Opportunity very shortly to drink a Health to the Muses, with some of the poetical Fraternity, and your self, who are Master of the Ceremonies to them; in the mean time, till I can recover the Duke's Papers, accept of the inclosed, from
Your real Friend and
humble Servant, &c.
Aug. 14, 1726.
P. S. A Simile, this Moment, occurs to my Memory, in a Speech from the QUEEN to the Duke of Norfolk, ex pede Herculem, viz.
Sure, were I free, and Norfolk was a Prisoner; I'd fly with more Impatience to his Arms, Than the poor Israelite gaz'd on the Serpent. When Life was the Reward of every Loak.

blocks.text: I.

paragraphs.text: I.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text:
CECILIA, celestial Maid,
To whom our annual Rites we pay,
Propitious hear our Vows, and hearing aid
On this thy own appropriated Day.
Sweet Harmony at thy Commands,
Shall tune our Tongues, and guide our Hands:
Our Tongues and Hands we now design,
In praise of Harmony, and Thee to join,
Harmonious Maid, for Harmony is Thine.
O Goddess of entrancing Measures,
Fautress of Concord, Peace and Love,
Gayest Joys, and safest Pleasures,
From thy Influence we prove:
Forbear a while the heavenly Choir,
Ours will be heavenly if thou inspire;
Musick shall wing our soaring Souls on high,
And bending Angels meet 'em from the Sky.

When gloomy Grief, or dark Despair Diltract the Head, the Bosom tear, And all the Racks of Rage appear, Then thou afferts the Empire of the Ear. At thy Command discording Passions cease, And the Soul sooths in Symphonies of Peace.
Thus when in heaviness of Heart,
David his Wretchednefsbemoan'd,
And almost funk beneath the Smart,
By Musick's magick Pow'r,
He fought to cure,
The Grief with which he groan'd.
But whilst he plays and whilst he fings,
At first in penitential plaintive Notes,
The mclancholy Mufick floats,
Along the sadly-founding Strings:
'Till by Degrees he found,
The sweet feraphick Sound,
Softly fliding through his Ears,
Lull his Anguish, calm his Cares,
And pour a Balm in every Wound.
Then with an Air,
Devoid of Care,
With swifter Fingers touch'd each String,
To louder Notes his Voice he rais'd,
And God, to whom before he Pray'd,he Prais'd.
CHORUS.
O Harmony, supremest Bliss. Which Men or Angels know, Angels dissolve in Ecstasies, And Men with Raptures glow.

III.
The solemn Organ now with Breath inspire, Whose all-commanding Sound Shall to the Skies rebound, The holy Heart with Transport fire, And Unbelief confound.
Now the full Notes in Peals ascend, And ratling shake the Dome,
The stubborn Wretch begins to bend,
Remorse and Guilt his aking Conscience rend
Preluding to the dreadful Blast to come.
* If Saints above,
In Songs of Love,
And Hymns of Praise,
Their Voices raife,
For one repentant Guest;
When each bleist Minstrel of the Sky, Joins in the universal Symphony,
To emulate the reft,
The sacred Organ's sound shall then prevail, And bright Cecilia crown the Festival.
CHORUS.
If Saints above,
In Songs of Love,
And Hymns of Praise,
Their Voices raise,
For one repentant Guest;
When each blest Minstrel of the Sky,
Joins in the universal Symphony,
To emulate the rest.
The sacred Organ's sound shall then prevail, And bright Cecilia crown the Festival.
*Alluding to that Passage, There is more Joy in Heaven over one Sinner that repents, than over ninety and nine just Persons who need no Repentance.

At first the Mountains gently seem to shake, Scarce conscious of the lubterraneous Wreck: 'Till the hot Vapours with collected Wrath, Join the distending Air, then bellowing forth The Mountain's fettled Basis they confound, And undistinguish'd Ruin deal around.
So when Love's fatal Darts our Breasts invade, Shot from the Glance of some relentless Maid, The infant Passion we with ease sustain.
Till the bright Nymph, as merciless as fair, Blows up the spreading Flame into Despair, Then Reason can no more our Hearts controll But universal Horror rends the Soul.

blocks.label: text
blocks.text: IF I did not believe your good Humour to be equal to your Wit, I should think you banter'd your Friend most unmercifully. I'm sure you would not charge me with a fault I am uncapable of committing, nor accuse me of running away with the Wit of the Town, if you had the same Opinion of me that I have of my self; for I also have hitherto been very much deceiv'd in my own Character, if there's any Body takes me for a Wit. That's a Title as far above my Ambition, as out of my Reach; and I have just the cunning of the Fox to cry four Grapes, when I can't come at them. I must confess I never so sensibly perceive'd the want of Wit as I do now, for it requires such a vast Fund to pay you in your own Coin, and to ballance the Accompts in Epistolary Commerce, that I shall certainly turn Bankrupt, unless you'll give large Credit, or, if need be, charitably forgive great Sums. The Satire against Wit, I remember, was for erecting a Wit-Bank in behalf of the poor Traders to the barren Coast. What advantage it would be to me, who have no Cash to put in, I know not, perhaps it might have furnish'd the Town with a Storehouse, that might have supply'd its wants all this Vacation. But it luckily falls out that in describing the dearth of Wit so ingeniously, you consute your self, as oftentimes the richest Men complain most of Poverty. Who can think 'tis scarce, when he sees it overflow so abundantly from your Pen? Lease

And tho' I know nothing of Mrs. Phillips but what I have learnt from her own Poems, I am confident she was discreet, good humour'd, modest, constant, and virtuous, as well as ingenious. Her Country Life is so sweet a Poem, and sprinkled with such profound philosophical Thoughts, express'd in easy poetical Language; or else by a kind of Sympathy it suits so well with my Sentiments and Inclination, that tho' I have read several Poems in more Tongues than one upon the same Subject, yet I don't know where to find a better. But whither am I running? Beyond my Lafte I'm sure; for I'm no more a Critick than a Wit or a Poet, leaving those Studies to such as practise them with more Success. And to a Friend I'll own, that Philosophy would be my darling, if I had either time, or strength, or opportunity, to pursue it with the application that it merits and requires: But I have neither, and therefore among the various noble Subjects, with which Philosophy entertains and improves the most exalted Minds, I shall chuse out one, which came from an Oracle, and in two words contains enough to employ all my idle Hours, which can be spar'd from the necessary Concerns of Life. It is Nosce TeIPSUM, (you understand it without an Interpreter). If the Subject be worthless and barren that's my fault, yet such as it is, I know none so little studied, and none so necessary and useful among all that employ the busy Minds of Men. --- My Humour and my Style exactly agree, and I write this with the most prevailing Passion of my Mind, next to my Esteem for Corinna. blocks.text: the better Understanding of Revealed Truths. This is the only good Use I can make of what little I have, or ever shall have, and I have so mean an Opinion of Human Learning abstractedly consider'd, that I reckon it only as you do, an innocent Amusement, which may serve to pass away some idle Hours now and then more agreeably than impertinent Conversation. Influenc'd by such Considerations as these, I chose my Nosce Teipsum, not as a Subject merely Philosophical, but in its largest extent, comprehending all the Duties of the Christian Religion. For he that rightly knows himself, will never be ignorant of his Duty to God and his Neighbour. And I pitch'd upon it the rather, because I think our most certain Knowledge proceeds from Reflection: And it gives me occasion with great Satisfaction to observe, how exactly Reason and Religion agree in every thing conducive to human Perfection and Happiness. Thus Corinna, at your request, for I can deny you nothing; I have given you the Result of my Philosophy. If you desire a farther account of my Religion, you may find it in Dr. Scot's Christian Life; whom I am more indebted to, and have a greater esteem for, than any uninspired Writer whatsoever. The Philosophy of the Christian Religion, and the Reason of all its Precepts is, in my Apprehension, so clearly taught, and so plainly prov'd in that divine Book, that he must want both Head and Heart, who can read it without being not almost, but altogether a Christian.
